name: Guardian genius crossword No 142
preamble: Seventeen solutions, not further defined in their clues, are partners in well-known pairings. The grid entry for these clues needs to be the other partner in the pair. Letter counts are for the word to be entered.

solutions.check: grid and clues read from the Guardian's article page and its grid picture, its numbering matching the clue list; each light's entry one fifteensquared prints for it, the only choice of them whose crossings all agree; an entry not its answer carries the answer as its alteration's `from`

indicators.note: to include something is to take it inside, so the motoring letters go within the others

blocks.note: one is I, and the 's is kept
C is the card-suit abbreviation for clubs
the AA is the Automobile Association, a British motoring organisation for drivers

explanation.surface: A golfer's bag holds clubs that include a couple of drivers.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay builds ISAAC, which per the preamble is not entered; the grid takes his partner in the pairing Abraham and Isaac, father and son in Genesis.
explanation.definitionFit: Undefined by the preamble: Isaac pairs with his father, the patriarch in Genesis who nearly sacrificed him.

indicators.note: one piece is set next to another, joined end to end in the order given

blocks.note: R is the abbreviation for right
the fish of the 1988 comedy film A Fish Called Wanda

explanation.surface: A claim of the right to film some fish.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay builds RWANDA; the grid takes its neighbour, since Rwanda and Burundi are the paired former Belgian territories of central Africa.
explanation.definitionFit: Undefined by the preamble: Rwanda's twin nation to the south, the two having been governed together as Ruanda-Urundi.

clue.text: The old revolutionary vow is binding

indicators.note: a revolution turns something right round, so the archaic word is read backwards
something binding wraps around another thing, so the pledge word goes round the other piece

blocks.note: a bond is a solemn pledge or promise
ye is the old form of 'the', as in Ye Olde Tea Shoppe

explanation.surface: An ageing revolutionary's oath holds him to the cause.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay builds BEYOND; the grid takes its partner in the phrase 'above and beyond', going further than duty requires.
explanation.definitionFit: Undefined by the preamble: beyond pairs with it in the idiom for exceeding what is expected.

indicators.note: to top something is to cut off its head, so the word loses its first letter

blocks.note: a partisan is a keen supporter of a cause

explanation.surface: Someone called Smith has done away with a fan.
explanation.walkthrough: Smith reads as a surname, but it is the craftsman who works metal.
explanation.definitionFit: A smith is a skilled manual worker in metal, so an example of a craftsperson.

indicators.note: novel means new and different, so the next word is given a fresh arrangement
one piece is placed inside the other

blocks.note: to be in a jam is to be in a mess or fix
the word is rearranged

explanation.surface: A new book is placed in a mess of some kind.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay builds JETSAM; the grid takes its partner in 'flotsam and jetsam', wreckage floating free and cargo thrown overboard.
explanation.definitionFit: Undefined by the preamble: jetsam is always coupled with the floating debris of a wreck in the stock phrase.

indicators.note: something worked is kneaded or shaped, so its letters are remoulded
the borders of a word are its two ends, so only its outer letters are kept
one piece is put into the other, so it sits inside

blocks.note: the first and last letters of the word
the word is rearranged

explanation.surface: A gardener works some ingredient into the flower borders.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay builds GENTLEMEN; the grid takes its partner in the formal address 'Ladies and gentlemen'.
explanation.definitionFit: Undefined by the preamble: gentlemen are coupled with women in the standard opening of a speech.

clue.text: Time to comfort half-hearted Republican fund manager

indicators.note: the heart of the word is its middle pair, and half of that pair is lost

blocks.note: T is the abbreviation for time
to reassure someone is to comfort them
R is the abbreviation for Republican

explanation.surface: A call to console a lukewarm American politician who runs a fund.
explanation.walkthrough: The middle of REASSURE is its double S, and half-hearted drops one of them.
explanation.definitionFit: A treasurer is the officer who looks after the money of a club, society or company.

clue.text: Made better finish — made different covers

indicators.note: made different means changed, so the letters of the word before it are rearranged
something that covers wraps round another, so one piece holds the other inside

blocks.note: the word is rearranged
the end is the finish

explanation.surface: Someone improved the ending, and a different version covers it.
explanation.walkthrough: The repeated word misleads: the first 'Made' belongs to the definition and the second is the anagram fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: To amend a text or law is to correct or improve it, so the past tense is a synonym.

indicators.note: comic means farcical and absurd, so the word before it is jumbled
something announced is spoken out, so the name counts by how it is said

blocks.note: the word is rearranged
Sir John Tenniel drew the original pictures for Alice in Wonderland

explanation.surface: A recent comic artist is announced for an anniversary celebration.
explanation.walkthrough: Tenniel, the Punch cartoonist who illustrated Lewis Carroll, fits the Looking-Glass theme of 11 across.
explanation.definitionFit: A tercentennial is a three-hundredth anniversary, the celebration marking three centuries.

clue.text: Musicians turn it on but not every second

indicators.note: every second letter is left out, so only the alternate ones count

blocks.note: the first, third, fifth and seventh letters of the phrase

explanation.surface: An instruction to switch the music on, though not continuously.
explanation.definitionFit: A trio is a group of three musicians playing together.

indicators.note: something terrible is in a dreadful state, so the following word is knocked into disorder

blocks.note: twee is a British word for over-pretty, sweet to the point of cloying
the word is jumbled

explanation.surface: Someone sighs that it is all a pretty terrible muddle.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay builds TWEEDLEDUM; the grid takes his twin from Through the Looking-Glass instead.
explanation.definitionFit: Undefined by the preamble: Tweedledum and Tweedledee are the quarrelling identical twins in Lewis Carroll's Looking-Glass story.

indicators.note: about means turned round, so the stuffing word is read from its end

blocks.note: to ram is to stuff or cram
x is the multiplication sign, read as times

explanation.surface: A dismissive verdict on what is written about in The Times.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay builds MARX; the grid takes his co-author of The Communist Manifesto, Friedrich Engels.
explanation.definitionFit: Undefined by the preamble: Marx and Engels are the paired founders of communist theory.

indicators.note: done mistakenly means put wrongly, so the letters come out in the wrong order

blocks.note: the answer to 10 across, its letters rearranged
L is the abbreviation for left
the newspaper setting the puzzle speaks of itself as us

explanation.surface: Three people wrongly walked out on the newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay builds TROILUS; the grid takes his faithless lover from Shakespeare's Troilus and Cressida.
explanation.definitionFit: Undefined by the preamble: Troilus is the Trojan prince whose love is the title partner in Shakespeare's play.

indicators.note: the margins of a word are its edges, so its first and last letters are taken
what is ignored is left out, so those letters are dropped from the newspaper

blocks.note: The Thunderer is a traditional nickname for The Times newspaper
the first and last letters of the word

explanation.surface: A newspaper is accused of overlooking the edges of its own mistakes.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay builds THUNDER; the grid takes its partner in 'thunder and lightning'.
explanation.definitionFit: Undefined by the preamble: thunder is the crash that follows the flash of an electrical storm.

blocks.note: H is slang for heroin
airlines are carriers of passengers

explanation.surface: Drug traffickers send a shockwave through the airline industry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shock' is not a jolt but a thick mass of hair, whose edges are hairlines.
explanation.definitionFit: A shock of hair is a thick head of it, and its edges along the forehead are the hairline.

indicators.note: to hire someone is to take them on, so one piece is taken inside the other

blocks.note: GM is the abbreviation for general manager
a roo, short for kangaroo, is an animal that bounces along

explanation.surface: A nightclub boss takes on a doorman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bouncer' looks like a doorman, but it is the kangaroo. The wordplay builds GROOM; the grid takes his partner at the wedding.
explanation.definitionFit: Undefined by the preamble: a groom is joined in marriage to the woman being wed beside him.

blocks.note: a gathering of men only is one with no women, and this word stands for that absence
W is the abbreviation for women, the ones excluded

explanation.surface: A question about a men-only club or magazine.
explanation.walkthrough: Men only means NO W, W being the abbreviation for women. The wordplay builds NOW; the grid takes its partner in 'now and again'.
explanation.definitionFit: Undefined by the preamble: now pairs with it in the idiom 'now and again', meaning occasionally.

clue.text: Firms join banks to create energy supplier

indicators.note: banks line a river on both sides, so one piece flanks the other

blocks.note: to glue things is to join them
Cos is the abbreviation for companies, or firms

explanation.surface: Companies merge with banks to form a new power company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'banks' is a verb here: GLUE flanks the companies on both sides.
explanation.definitionFit: Glucose is the sugar the body burns for fuel, so it supplies the cells with energy.

clue.text: Serious change in speed, then another

indicators.note: a change in something alters its make-up, so the letters are rearranged
then means next, so the second piece follows the first

blocks.note: the word is rearranged
another word for speed, as in rate of knots

explanation.surface: A driver makes a major change of pace and then another.
explanation.walkthrough: 'another' points back to speed: the second piece is another word meaning speed.
explanation.definitionFit: A desperate situation is grave and critical, so desperate can mean very serious.

clue.text: Groom pauses, harnessing head of grey horse

indicators.note: to groom is to brush and tidy up, so the letters are put into new order
harnessing yokes an extra letter into the mix before it is rearranged
the head of a word is its first letter

blocks.note: taken as written, to be mixed
the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A stable groom stops for a moment while putting the harness on a grey horse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Groom' reads as the stable hand, but it is the instruction to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Pegasus is the winged horse of Greek myth, born from the blood of Medusa.

indicators.note: to intercept is to cut in on something, so one piece lands inside the other

blocks.note: a pilot scheme is a trial run
the V-1 was the German flying bomb of the Second World War

explanation.surface: A small missile shoots down an aircraft's pilot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pilot' is not the flyer but the adjective in pilot scheme.
explanation.definitionFit: Something lightweight is of little importance or substance, which is what trivial means.

clue.text: Programme broadcast shot around very start of war

indicators.note: broadcast means scattered widely, as seed is sown, so the letters are strewn into a new order
the jumbled word goes around the next piece, holding it inside
the start of a word is its first letter

blocks.note: the word is rearranged
V is the abbreviation for very
the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A programme airs footage shot right at the outbreak of war.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broadcast' sits naturally beside 'Programme', but it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A TV show is a programme made for television.

indicators.note: a thief who steals takes things in, so the other letters end up inside

blocks.note: Gert and Daisy were a British comedy double act of the 1930s and 40s, played by the Waters sisters
the Roman numeral for one
lb is the abbreviation for a pound in weight

explanation.surface: Daisy's other half pockets a single pound coin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'partner' looks like the theme's signal but is wordplay, Daisy's comic partner Gert. The wordplay builds GILBERT; the grid takes his partner in the comic opera duo.
explanation.definitionFit: Undefined by the preamble: W S Gilbert wrote the words and Arthur Sullivan the music of the Savoy operas.

blocks.note: a wall is what a bricklayer builds; the question mark flags the loose link
an ace is an expert

explanation.surface: A query whether someone is a skilled builder.
explanation.walkthrough: An expert bricklayer is an ace at walls, a WALL ACE. The wordplay builds WALLACE; the grid takes his dog in the Aardman animations Wallace and Gromit.
explanation.definitionFit: Undefined by the preamble: Wallace is the cheese-loving inventor whose silent beagle is his constant companion.

indicators.note: something that holds another keeps it inside

blocks.note: A-ha! is the catchphrase of Alan Partridge, Steve Coogan's comic chat-show host
an LP is a long-playing record

explanation.surface: A partridge's cry contains a record of birdsong.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Partridge' reads as the bird, but it is the TV character. The wordplay builds ALPHA; the grid takes its partner in 'alpha and omega'.
explanation.definitionFit: Undefined by the preamble: alpha and omega are the first and last letters of the Greek alphabet, the beginning and the end.

indicators.note: to entertain guests is to have them in, so one piece takes in the other

blocks.note: speleologists explore caves
Muhammad Ali, the heavyweight champion

explanation.surface: Cave explorers play host to a boxer.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay builds CAVALIERS; the grid takes their opponents in the English Civil War, the Parliamentarian Roundheads.
explanation.definitionFit: Undefined by the preamble: the Royalist Cavaliers fought Parliament's cropped-haired soldiers in the 1640s.

indicators.note: to ban something is to shut it out, so those letters are removed

blocks.note: Charles Gounod composed the opera Faust
un is the French indefinite article, his being the Frenchman's

explanation.surface: A French composer outlaws one of his own pieces.
explanation.walkthrough: 'his' makes the article French. The wordplay builds GOOD; the grid takes its opposite in 'good and evil'.
explanation.definitionFit: Undefined by the preamble: good is morally right, and is paired with its wicked opposite.

clue.text: Yo-yos used to be around in places like York

indicators.note: turned around means facing the other way, so the words are read backwards
one piece is placed inside the other

blocks.note: York is the seat of an archbishop, and a bishop's seat is a see
was is the past of be

explanation.surface: Toys that used to be found around cities like York.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yo-yos' is a verb, and 'York' is a cathedral city rather than a place in general.
explanation.definitionFit: To yo-yo is to go up and down repeatedly, as a seesaw does, so the verbs share a sense of fluctuating.

clue.text: Milliner in Bow appears in Times

indicators.note: Bow is in London's Cockney East End, where speakers drop the H at the start of a word
to appear in something is to be seen inside it

blocks.note: by means times, as in three by four
a milliner makes hats, as a hatter does

explanation.surface: A hatmaker from the East End appears in a newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay builds BATTERY; the grid takes its partner in the legal phrase 'assault and battery'.
explanation.definitionFit: Undefined by the preamble: battery is unlawful physical contact, charged alongside the threat of it.
